blocks.text: Model introduction

“Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I understand you are considering an intrauterine contraceptive device. I would like to discuss your pregnancy-prevention goals, medical history, menstrual cycle and any concerns you may have. I will explain how the device works, its benefits and risks, and what insertion and removal involve. You can ask questions at any time, and the decision will be yours. Is that alright?”

A. Copper-bearing IUCD
Examples include the Copper T 380A and other copper-bearing devices.

The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) is a different device and will be discussed in Station 153.

blocks.text: Exam distinction: a copper IUCD is hormone-free and may increase menstrual bleeding; an LNG-IUS releases a hormone and commonly reduces menstrual bleeding.
The copper IUCD prevents pregnancy mainly by impairing sperm function and fertilisation.

items.text: Copper ions and the local uterine inflammatory response impair sperm motility, viability and ability to fertilise an ovum.
The local environment within the uterus and reproductive tract makes fertilisation highly unlikely.
The device does not primarily work by suppressing ovulation.

blocks.text: The copper IUD is not an abortifacient. It prevents fertilisation and does not terminate an established pregnancy.
The copper IUCD is one of the most effective reversible contraceptive methods, with fewer than one pregnancy per 100 users in the first year.

The device may partially or completely come out of the uterus. If expulsion occurs, contraceptive protection may be lost.
Perforation is uncommon but may occur during insertion. Risk assessment and correct technique are important, particularly in postpartum settings.

There is a small increased risk of pelvic infection around the time of insertion, particularly when an untreated cervical infection is present. The long-term risk is low in the absence of an ongoing infection.

Pregnancy with an IUCD in situ is uncommon. However, if pregnancy occurs, assess urgently for ectopic pregnancy because the proportion of pregnancies that are ectopic is higher among the rare pregnancies occurring with an IUD in place.
The IUD does not necessarily increase the overall risk of ectopic pregnancy; it substantially reduces pregnancy overall.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. When is the copper IUCD effective?

blocks.text: The copper IUCD provides contraceptive protection immediately after correct insertion.
It can also be used for emergency contraception.

A copper IUD can generally be inserted within five days of unprotected intercourse. In some circumstances, insertion may be possible more than five days after intercourse if it is no more than five days after estimated ovulation, according to the applicable guideline.
It is the most effective established emergency contraceptive method and can provide ongoing contraception after insertion.

The IUCD can be removed whenever she requests it.

items.text: Perform a pregnancy test.

If the device is not identified in the uterus, further imaging, commonly an abdominal and pelvic X-ray, may be required to determine whether it has been expelled or has migrated outside the uterus.

blocks.text: Step 4 — Management

items.text: If the device is correctly positioned and the patient wants to continue using it, the threads may not need to be retrieved.
If removal is requested or clinically indicated, use appropriate instruments and expertise.
If the device is not located, arrange further investigation and specialist assessment.
If expulsion is suspected, advise backup contraception and assess the need for emergency contraception based on recent intercourse.
If pregnancy is confirmed, assess urgently for ectopic pregnancy where appropriate.

blocks.text: Critical OSCE point: never assume that missing threads mean the IUCD has been expelled.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. Pregnancy with an IUCD in situ

blocks.text: Although pregnancy is rare with an IUCD, it requires prompt assessment.

items.text: Last menstrual period and pregnancy symptoms.
Pelvic or abdominal pain.
Vaginal bleeding.
Dizziness, collapse or shoulder-tip pain.
IUCD type and insertion date.
Pregnancy test.
Quantitative serum β-hCG where clinically indicated.
Transvaginal ultrasound to establish the location of the pregnancy and assess the IUCD.
Exclude ectopic pregnancy urgently. A patient with pain, haemodynamic instability, collapse or significant bleeding needs emergency assessment.
If the pregnancy is intrauterine, discuss the patient's pregnancy intentions and the risks associated with leaving the IUCD in place.

If the patient wishes to continue the pregnancy, arrange obstetric or gynaecological assessment. If the threads are visible or the device can be removed safely from the cervical canal, early removal is generally recommended when feasible.
If the threads are not visible, do not attempt blind removal. Arrange specialist management.
If the patient does not wish to continue the pregnancy, provide non-judgmental counselling and appropriate care according to her wishes and local law.

blocks.text: Leaving an IUCD in place during an ongoing pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage, septic miscarriage, infection and preterm birth. Removal, when safely feasible, reduces some of these risks.
Features

items.text: Threads become longer or the device becomes visible at the cervix.

The patient feels part of the device in the vagina.
Pregnancy may occur if protection is lost.

subsections.subsection_title: 15. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the mechanism of action of the copper IUCD?
Copper impairs sperm motility, viability and fertilising capacity, producing a local environment that makes fertilisation highly unlikely.
Q2. What is the major disadvantage of the copper IUCD?
Heavier menstrual bleeding and increased dysmenorrhoea, particularly during the initial months.
Q3. Can a nulliparous woman use an IUCD?
Yes. Nulliparity alone is not a contraindication.
Q4. What would you do if the IUCD threads were missing?
Take a history, perform a speculum examination, test for pregnancy and arrange ultrasound. If the device is not identified in the uterus, further imaging may be necessary. Avoid blind retrieval.
Q5. Can a copper IUCD be used as emergency contraception?
Yes. It can generally be inserted within five days of unprotected intercourse, with additional timing options in selected circumstances based on estimated ovulation and applicable guidance.
Q6. What is the risk of infection after insertion?

The risk is generally low. There is a small increased risk around insertion, particularly when an untreated cervical infection is present. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not generally required for uncomplicated insertion.
Q7. What is the management of pregnancy with an IUCD in situ?

Confirm pregnancy, urgently assess for ectopic pregnancy when appropriate, establish pregnancy location by ultrasound and arrange specialist counselling. If the pregnancy is to continue, early removal is generally recommended when the threads are visible or the device can be safely retrieved.
Q8. Does the copper IUCD cause permanent infertility?
No. Fertility generally returns promptly after removal. Untreated pelvic infection, rather than the correctly used device itself, can damage the reproductive tract.
